words.def: To stop doing something or leave something behind.
words.note: Say abandon a plan, not abandon from a plan. The verb doesn't need a preposition.

col.en: We had to *abandon* the plan because it was too expensive.
Don't *abandon* the idea just because it's difficult.
Don't *abandon* hope. Things can still change.
They decided to *abandon* the project.

words.def: The skill or power to do something.

col.p_ar: تكون عندك القدرة باش دير شي حاجة
col.en: She has the *ability* to solve problems quickly.
The job requires the *ability* to learn quickly.
He has a natural *ability* to communicate with people.
This course will help you develop your *abilities*.

words.def: Having the skill, knowledge or opportunity to do something.
words.note: Say I can help you or I'm able to help you, not I am can help you. Don't combine can and able to.

col.en: I'll be *able* to help you tomorrow.
I'm not *able* to access my account.
After the update, you'll be *able* to use the new features.

col.p_ar: تكون قادر مادياً تشري شي حاجة
col.en: She isn't *able* to afford a new laptop right now.

words.def: Connected to a subject; approximately; nearly ready to do something.
words.note: Say talk about something, not talk on something when discussing a general topic.

col.en: We need to talk *about* your problem.
I don't know much *about* computers.
I'm *about* to leave.
What *about* the other option?
The update will take *about* 20 minutes.

words.def: At a higher level or position; more than a particular amount.
words.note: Say above the table, not on above the table. Don't use both prepositions together.

col.en: His English is *above* average.
*Above* all, be patient with customers.
As mentioned *above*, the system needs an update.
Your internet usage is *above* the limit.

words.note: Say go abroad, not go to abroad. Abroad doesn't need to.

col.en: I want to go *abroad* to study.
She's planning to study *abroad* next year.
Many people want to work *abroad*.
My cousin lives *abroad*.

words.def: Complete or total; with no limits or exceptions.
words.note: This word is less common in casual conversation than words like complete or total.

col.en: I'm an *absolute* beginner in French.
Nobody can say that with *absolute* certainty.
There was *absolute* silence in the room.
My desk is an *absolute* mess.

words.def: Completely; used to strongly agree or say yes.
words.note: Say absolutely sure, not very absolutely sure. Absolutely already makes the meaning stronger.

col.en: You're *absolutely* right about that.
Are you *absolutely* sure?

col.p_ar: مزيان تماماً / ما كاين حتى مشكل
col.en: That's *absolutely* fine with me.
Would you share your password? *Absolutely* not!

words.def: Related to education, schools or universities; an academic is someone who teaches or researches at a university.
words.note: Academic is common in education and formal writing. In everyday conversation, people often say university or school instead.

col.en: The *academic* year starts in September.
Regular practice can improve your *academic* performance.
What's your *academic* background?
She's interested in *academic* research.
He's an *academic* at a British university.

words.def: To say yes to something offered or suggested; to agree to receive or take something.

col.en: She decided to *accept* the job offer.
You should *accept* responsibility for your mistakes.
The manager *accepted* my request.
You need to *accept* the fact that learning takes time.
I hope she'll *accept* my apology.

texts.title: Text 1 – A hard decision
texts.en:
Sara had a big plan: she wanted to open a small shop. She talked *about* it with her family for weeks. But the rent was *above* her budget, so she had to *abandon* the plan. At first she felt sad.

Then her brother said, "You have the *ability* to learn fast. You will be *able* to try again." In the end, Sara decided to *accept* a job in a bookshop. "I will never *abandon* hope," she said.

texts.title: Text 2 – Studying abroad
texts.en:
Omar is an *absolute* beginner in German, but he wants to study *abroad* next year. His *academic* record is good, and his teacher says he is *absolutely* ready.

"Are you *absolutely* sure?" his mother asked. "Yes," said Omar. "The *academic* year starts in September, and I will be *able* to learn the language fast. Let's talk *about* it tonight."
